title: Sell Mineral Rights in Johnson County, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Johnson County, WY
metaDescription: Johnson County, WY mineral owner near Buffalo, Kaycee, or the Powder River Basin's southern edge? Get a fair, no-obligation cash offer.
heroLead: Johnson County sits on the southwestern flank of the Powder River Basin, Buffalo as the county seat, Kaycee and Hole-in-the-Wall country to the south, and a mineral estate driven by everything from historic cattle range wars to modern horizontal drilling.
intro: Ranchers here have always understood that what's above the ground and what's below it are two different kinds of property. That understanding got written into deeds generations ago, when families sold the surface during hard years but kept the minerals, or vice versa, and it's still working its way through probate courts and county clerk filings today.

If you're holding a Johnson County mineral interest, whether it's producing under an active horizontal unit or sitting quiet on ground your family homesteaded a century ago, the starting point is always the same: figure out exactly what you own before you talk about what it's worth.

sections.heading: The basin's southwestern edge
paragraphs: Johnson County sits where the Powder River Basin's productive Niobrara, Turner, Sussex, and Parkman formations begin to thin toward the basin margin near the Bighorn Mountains. Activity here has historically been lighter than the core counties to the north and east, Campbell and Converse, but horizontal drilling has periodically extended south and west into Johnson County acreage as operators chase remaining productive rock.

That means ownership patterns here range widely, some tracts sit inside active, producing spacing units with regular royalty checks, while others nearby have never drawn a lease. Location relative to the current drilling front matters more here than almost anywhere else in the basin.

sections.heading: Kaycee, Hole-in-the-Wall, and the county's ranching backbone
paragraphs: The southern part of the county, around Kaycee and the Hole-in-the-Wall country made famous by outlaw history, has stayed heavily ranching-focused, with oil and gas activity concentrated in specific fields rather than blanketing the landscape. Barnum field and similar legacy structures have produced for decades in this area, alongside newer horizontal targets.

Ranch families throughout Johnson County commonly hold mineral interests that trace back to original homestead patents from the early 1900s, sometimes with minerals reserved when the surface was later sold to a neighboring operation or a new owner. Untangling exactly which generation severed what from what is often the real work in preparing a mineral tract for sale.

sections.heading: Split estate and federal minerals
paragraphs: A meaningful share of Johnson County's subsurface is federally owned, minerals reserved to the United States under the Stock-Raising Homestead Act even where the surface is privately owned and ranched. If your family's patent came through that route, you may own the surface without owning what's underneath it, a split estate situation that's common across this part of Wyoming and not a defect in your title, just a different kind of ownership.

Confirming whether your specific tract is privately owned minerals or federally reserved minerals is the single most important step before pricing any interest, since only privately held minerals are yours to sell.

sections.heading: Reading a Johnson County royalty statement
paragraphs: Horizontal wells in this part of the basin typically show a strong first-year decline followed by a longer, flatter stripper-style tail, which means your check five years into a well's life will look very different from your first one, without anything having gone wrong. Buyers price interests against that decline curve, not against your best month.

Bring your most recent two or three check stubs, your division order, and your original mineral deed when you're ready to get a real number instead of a guess. If your interest has never produced, bring your deed and legal description instead, and expect a more conservative, speculative valuation reflecting undeveloped acreage rather than an active royalty stream.

faqs.question: How do I find out if I own surface or mineral rights in Johnson County?
faqs.answer: Pull your deed and any patent records through the Johnson County Clerk's office in Buffalo. Stock-Raising Homestead Act patents commonly reserved minerals to the federal government even where the surface passed to private ownership.

faqs.question: Is horizontal drilling active in Johnson County right now?
faqs.answer: Activity has extended into parts of the county from the more heavily drilled areas to the north and east, but it's not uniform. Check current permits and unit filings for your specific section through the Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Kaycee-area production and the rest of the county?
faqs.answer: The Kaycee and Hole-in-the-Wall area sits closer to legacy fields like Barnum, with a mix of older vertical and newer horizontal activity, while other parts of the county may have seen little to no drilling depending on proximity to the basin's productive core.

faqs.question: My family has owned this ranch for four generations, do we automatically own the minerals?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Long ownership of the surface doesn't guarantee mineral ownership if a prior generation sold or reserved them separately, or if the original federal patent excluded minerals entirely. A title check clarifies this before any sale.

faqs.question: Can I sell just part of my Johnson County mineral interest?
faqs.answer: Yes, partial interest sales are common, whether that's a percentage of your ownership or minerals under a specific portion of your acreage. Talk through what you want to retain before structuring the sale.
